extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; educated early-18th-century English public (gentlemen, citizens, people interested in manners and morals)
extracted.subtask_description: A short early-18th-century periodical essay giving moral and social judgments about manners, conduct, and character (e.g., pleasure-seekers, soldiers, youth/age, courtship). Often mixes anecdote, exhortation, and prescriptive examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of being a Man of Pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man of Pleasure sacrifices severity and delicacy of passions to appetites; he is complacent and unconcerned, seeks immediate gratifications, and fails to observe the long-term harms of pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure 'looks' charming as it approaches but departs leaving 'Disorder, Impotence, down-cast Shame, and conscious Imperfection.' The pursuit of pleasure makes 'Youth inglorious, Age shameful.' Practical consequences include negligence as friend/father/husband, mortgages, diseases, settlements, and eventual poverty for his descendants; many who end at Tyburn were formerly men of wit and pleasure. Avoid intemperate meals, excessive drinking, smoking, and roaring; reflect on actions rather than chase momentary mirth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irresolution and Procrastination as symptoms of Pleasure-addiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Addiction to pleasure produces irresolution and procrastination across a man's affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such indecisiveness brings dishonour to gentlemen and bankruptcy to traders; the habit degrades diligence and leads to social and economic ruin. Recognize these as natural effects of a life devoted to delight and correct by cultivating steadiness and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal tolerance for talented libertines
rubrics_metrics.description: Some men of great talents have been sacrificed to pleasure, and their shining qualities have made their vices appear attractive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why society sometimes forgives libertine behaviour: wit and genius can 'recommend Madness.' But such exceptions should not license general indulgence; the elegant qualities of a few do not justify the ruinous effects on most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical Courage versus Reasoned (Heroick) Courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the crowd-born, habitual 'mechanick' courage of ordinary soldiers from the reasoned, principle-based courage of true commanders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical courage arises from acting always in a crowd and seeing many survive; it lacks reflection and does not make great commanders. True leaders attain a resignation to death through reasoning about greater goods and duty: they accept that 'it is one Day to be resigned' and hazard life in pursuit of virtue and the common good. Evaluate courage by whether it springs from habit or from principled deliberation about duty and glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of shallow friendship among soldiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Companionship that shows indifference at calamity reveals shallow affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: when one rider drowns, a companion's casual 'he had a mad Horse' epitaph indicates lack of genuine attachment. True comrades in arms show compassion and personal concern, not indifference. Assess friendship by responses to fellow-soldiers' danger and loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of the honourable military commander
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'fine gentleman' or leader in a regiment is foremost in danger, beloved by officers and soldiers, just in distribution, modest in consumption, and ready to hazard himself for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He treats officers as friends and privates as brethren, inspires mutual love, avoids rapacity (would 'think himself below the most rapacious Agent' to enjoy a farthing above pay), and is generous and just. Such conduct yields 'immortal Glory' and is the ideal for command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper attitude toward ageing
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unworthy and irrational for a well-educated person to wish to be younger; age brings its own dignities and rational pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wishing for youth is often prompted by memory of shameful or impossible repetitions, or by mere desire for bodily strength. Reason counsels contentment: years enlarge capacities for rational pleasures (good fame, contemplation, respect), memory of a well-spent youth gives peaceful pleasure, and age should be embraced as preferable when virtuous. 'He that would be long an old Man, must begin early to be one.' Cultivate habits early that make ageing noble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding regret for youthful follies
rubrics_metrics.description: An old man who laments the loss of youthful gratifications demonstrates irrational self-pity and disordered appetites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old age should be a time of enlarged rational enjoyment; if one cannot look back with satisfaction, one should at least be free from temptation to repeat follies. Resignation to the natural course of life and focus on rational pleasures corrects this vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advice for young gentlemen to win women
rubrics_metrics.description: Young men of good education should attend to small deportments — entrance air, audacity with gaiety and grace — to be agreeable to women and to compete with impudent men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sober, modest man may be dismissed as 'precise' unless he improves in minor social skills: a good air on entering a room, a proper audacity in expression, and graceful gaiety make him attractive. Practice these 'little things' to avoid being outshone by rakes and impudent fellows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indecent licence in public discourse toward women is unacceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: It is indecent for men to take liberties of immodest talk or ribaldry in the presence of women who cannot avoid hearing it (e.g., shopkeepers, milliners, coffee-house keepers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such behaviour insults modest women who must attend to customers; it reduces their cheerfulness and harms their business prospects. Men should show deference in public, understand the passive suffering of tradeswomen, and avoid interpreting looks or gestures with sexualized imagination. The essay urges publicly arguing for decency and possibly shaming offenders by recording their words.

rubrics_metrics.name: The harm of treating women as mere attractions in commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: When women with natural attractions are treated as spectacles rather than customers, their prospects for marriage or honest maintenance suffer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mercenary treatment is a social mischief: men who toy with women in shops may divert custom, damage a woman's credit and marriage chances, and fail to protect her in bankruptcy or misfortune. Men of honour should act to preserve women's reputation and livelihood; decorum in commerce matters morally and economically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits and performance of a successful 'Woman's Man'
rubrics_metrics.description: A woman's man fashions himself differently from other men: loose, negligent garb; soft, indolent manner; little officious attentions; knowledge of family matters; readiness to entertain and ingratiate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success with the fair sex often depends on singularity, whim, and 'a Faculty of arguing' rather than sound judgment. The woman's man imitates aspects of the woman he hopes to win (metaphorically 'imitates their voices'), displays petty officiousness (knows what to do for a cold, carries spirits), keeps an air of inconstancy while being witty and humorous, and cultivates a reputation for being 'well with other women.' These affectations, not virtue, win favour among certain women.

rubrics_metrics.name: The strategic cultivation of reputation among women
rubrics_metrics.description: To please a particular woman it helps to be reputed to be favoured by other women; rivalry and imitation amplify success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A little spite or suspicion that a man is liked by rivals increases his desirability; fashion and opposition lead women to imitate one another's choices. For a would-be favourite cultivate wit, inconstancy, a lively tongue, and the appearance of being desired by others — but recognize the moral emptiness of such artifice.
